result: At a 5% false-alarm rate and a 2-minute deadline, DeepQCD catches 83–95% of the TWAP, passive-skew, short-gamma and lean episodes, and alarms after only 5% of news jumps. A window-limited CUSUM given a model of each policy catches 94% of instant unwinds (DeepQCD 54%) and 75% of TWAPs, but few of the passive ones. A flow z-score catches at most 20% of anything, and no detector sees a quote withdrawal. Detecting is not the same as profiting: only the aggressive unwinds leave the price away from value. Fading a detected instant unwind earns about 4 ticks over 5 minutes when market makers skew their quotes openly, and nothing measurable when they skew discreetly.

edge.1.00: With open skewing, an instant unwind has pushed the price 2–3 ticks from value by the time it is detected. Fading it after the alarm earns about 4 ticks over 5 minutes after cost: +3.7 ± 1.9 for DeepQCD and +4.4 ± 1.4 for the CUSUM. TWAP and the passive policies leave the price close to value; they are easy to detect but leave little or nothing to fade. Alarms after news point the wrong way: the price is still 13–20 ticks short of the news, and fading loses about 12 ticks within a minute.
edge.0.25: With discreet skewing, instant unwinds still leave the price 3–4 ticks from value at the alarm, but fading them is no longer profitable within the standard errors (−4.7 ± 2.8 for DeepQCD, −1.2 ± 1.5 for the CUSUM over 5 minutes). Passive unwinds again leave the price at value. Detection holds up while the trading edge disappears. In this market, detecting another maker's stress is more useful for managing one's own quotes than for trading against it.

limits:
• The edge is partly built in. Price impact and its decay (λ and η) are our assumptions, and the reversion that makes fading profitable follows from them. Real impact is concave in size and decays slowly. Real market makers also hide inventory better than a linear quote skew does; the discreet scenario is one step in that direction.
  • Only the level and volatility are calibrated. They come from the S&P 500 (FRED). Order arrival rates, sizes, the number and quoting of market makers, and the stress policies are chosen, not fitted. The spread is one tick, as in E-mini futures, but the book is far thinner than the real one.
  • Real labelled data is the real test. Crypto futures exchanges publish every forced liquidation as it happens (for example Binance's forceOrder stream), next to their public order books; academic order-book data (LOBSTER for Nasdaq, CME market-by-order) can be matched with known events. Training here and testing there would show what transfers.
  • Which policy, not which firm. The label here is that some maker is under stress. Telling the policies apart is a multi-class version of the same network. Telling which firm it is cannot be done from anonymous data, and is not the aim.
  • Use. Inferring stress from public market data is ordinary market analysis; trading on non-public order information, or creating false signals, is not. The most direct use is defensive: widen, shrink or step back when another maker is unwinding.
